clue.text: People who are naturally jumpy might find them superfluous

definitions.text: People who are naturally jumpy might find them superfluous

parts.words: People who are naturally jumpy might find them superfluous
parts.note: anyone with springs in their legs would have no need of a board to bounce off when diving or vaulting

explanation.surface: A dry remark that nervous, jumpy people need no extra help to leap about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumpy' reads as nervous, but here it means literally good at jumping, so the boards that launch divers and gymnasts would be wasted on them.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the flexible planks that divers and gymnasts bounce from to gain height.

clue.text: Lord High Everything Else

parts.note: the comic title held by the pompous official in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Mikado, who holds every office going

explanation.surface: A grand mock title for someone who holds every post at once.
explanation.walkthrough: In Gilbert and Sullivan's operetta The Mikado, the character holds all the state offices nobody else wants and is styled Lord High Everything Else.
explanation.definitionFit: The character's name became a general term for a self-important person holding many offices.

clue.text: Latin dice (anag.)

indicators.note: the bracketed abbreviation for anagram tells the solver to rearrange the two words before it

explanation.surface: Reads as an instruction about Roman gaming dice.
explanation.walkthrough: In 1940s Times puzzles a bare '(anag.)' clue gave no definition at all: the answer is simply the one sensible word the letters of LATIN DICE make.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue carries no separate definition, so the answer is just the word meaning exactly alike that the letters spell.

clue.text: Dashing fellows all in French gloves

indicators.note: the word all sits inside the French word for gloves

parts.note: gants is French for gloves

explanation.surface: Stylish young men all decked out in French gloves.
explanation.definitionFit: Gallants are fashionable, spirited young men about town, the dashing sort.

clue.text: He made the planets go like clockwork

definitions.text: He made the planets go like clockwork

parts.words: He made the planets go like clockwork
parts.note: the clockwork model of the solar system was named after the Earl of ..., for whom an early one was built

explanation.surface: Praise for some god-like figure who set the heavens running smoothly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He' suggests a creator or astronomer; the answer is both the earl's title and the geared planetarium named after him.
explanation.definitionFit: A mechanical planetarium whose clockwork gears move model planets round the sun, named after the Earl.

clue.text: There may be virtue in the left

definitions.text: There may be virtue in the left

parts.words: There may be virtue in the left
parts.note: a saint's bones or belongings are what is left behind, and were believed to hold healing virtue

explanation.surface: Reads like a political claim that the left wing may have its merits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The left' looks political, but means what is left over, the remains of a saint, thought to carry miraculous power.
explanation.definitionFit: A holy remnant of a saint, such as a bone, venerated for its supposed power.

clue.text: Stephenson's aeroplane, if he had invented one

definitions.text: Stephenson's aeroplane, if he had invented one

parts.words: Stephenson's aeroplane, if he had invented one
parts.note: George Stephenson's famous locomotive was the Rocket, so a flying version would be a rocket in the sky

explanation.surface: An idle what-if about the railway pioneer turning to aviation.
explanation.walkthrough: Stephenson's engine was called the Rocket; one that flew would be a rocket of the sky, which is also a firework.
explanation.definitionFit: A firework that shoots high into the air, punningly a flying version of the locomotive.

clue.text: Not Walton's spelling

parts.note: Izaak Walton, author of The Compleat Angler, spelt his first name with a Z and a K, unlike the usual form

explanation.surface: A pedant's note that some word is not spelt the way Walton spelt it.
explanation.walkthrough: The angling writer spelt his name Izaak; the clue wants the ordinary spelling of that first name.
explanation.definitionFit: The standard spelling of the Biblical first name that the angler wrote differently.

clue.text: It has been said that man is the only animal that does, or needs to

definitions.text: It has been said that man is the only animal that does, or needs to

parts.words: It has been said that man is the only animal that does, or needs to
parts.note: Mark Twain wrote that man is the only animal that reddens in the face with shame, or needs to

explanation.surface: A quoted aphorism about human uniqueness and human guilt.
explanation.walkthrough: The line is Mark Twain's; the missing verb is what people do when embarrassed.
explanation.definitionFit: To redden in the face from shame or embarrassment, the act Twain said only humans perform.

clue.text: The stoker's bird

parts.note: a stoker spends his day heaving coal with a spade, and there is a duck named for its spade-like bill

explanation.surface: Suggests a pet kept by a ship's fireman.
explanation.walkthrough: The duck takes its name from its broad, spade-like bill; a stoker is one who wields a spade on coal.
explanation.definitionFit: A dabbling duck with a broad spatulate bill, and also anyone who works with a spade.

clue.text: "That sober freedom out of which there springs Our 'passion for our temperate kings "(Tennyson)

definitions.text: "That sober freedom out of which there springs Our 'passion for our temperate kings "(Tennyson)

parts.words: "That sober freedom out of which there springs Our 'passion for our temperate kings "(Tennyson)
parts.note: the quotation has a word missing before passion, the adjective Tennyson used for devoted, faithful feeling towards the crown

explanation.surface: A fill-in-the-blank from Tennyson's patriotic verse about measured liberty and kingship.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap, marked by the stray apostrophe, falls before 'passion': Tennyson wrote of a faithful passion for temperate kings.
explanation.definitionFit: Faithful and devoted to a sovereign, the feeling the poet says sober freedom produces.

clue.text: As the fish-bait said in its round

definitions.meaning: the worm on the hook might complain I ..., meaning it has been bitten
a round is a circuit or scope, the area something reaches

explanation.surface: A talking worm on a hook, remarking on its turn at fishing.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as two words, the answer is the bait's complaint 'am bit', bitten by the fish; whole, it means a compass or circuit.
explanation.definitionFit: Scope, extent or circuit of something, the round it covers.

clue.text: Nature of. Pitt's crime

parts.note: Pitt the Elder, mocked in Parliament for his youth

explanation.surface: Asks what sort of offence a Prime Minister committed.
explanation.walkthrough: The reference is Pitt the Elder's famous retort about 'the atrocious crime of being a young man'.
explanation.definitionFit: Wicked or appalling, the adjective Pitt applied ironically to his youth.

clue.text: They get so confused, at chess

indicators.note: these letters are thrown into disorder, as muddled as the creatures squabbling

explanation.surface: Players who become thoroughly muddled during a game of chess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'They' seems to mean chess players; it is the female felines, and 'get so confused' rearranges AT CHESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Female felines, the 'they' of the clue, known for squalling quarrels.

clue.text: Dickensian shell fish

definitions.meaning: Nathaniel ... is one of the Pickwick Club members in Dickens's Pickwick Papers
a small edible sea snail, picked from its shell with a pin

explanation.surface: A seafood dish described as belonging to the world of Dickens.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a Pickwickian sportsman in Dickens and a small edible sea snail.

clue.text: A lost ruin (anag.)

indicators.note: the bracketed abbreviation for anagram tells the solver to rearrange the three words before it

explanation.surface: Suggests some vanished ancient remains.
explanation.walkthrough: The stray 6 is a printing slip: A LOST RUIN has exactly the nine letters needed. Like other bare '(anag.)' clues of the period, it gives no definition.
explanation.definitionFit: There is no separate definition; the letters make the word for a material that blocks heat or current.

clue.text: Bohemian composer, but not of that girl

definitions.text: Bohemian composer, but not of that girl

parts.words: Bohemian composer, but not of that girl
parts.note: the Irishman Balfe wrote the opera The Bohemian Girl; this man was a composer from Bohemia itself, not the author of that work

explanation.surface: Seems to ask who composed the once-famous opera The Bohemian Girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bohemian composer' calls Balfe's opera The Bohemian Girl to mind, but the clue rules him out: it wants a composer who really was Bohemian, the Czech author of Má vlast.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedřich, the Czech nationalist composer born in Bohemia, writer of The Bartered Bride.

clue.text: "Wise men know well enough what -——you make of them" (Hamlet)

definitions.text: "Wise men know well enough what -——you make of them" (Hamlet)

parts.words: "Wise men know well enough what -——you make of them" (Hamlet)
parts.note: Hamlet tells Ophelia that wise men know what horned beasts wives make of husbands, a jibe about cuckolds

explanation.surface: A Shakespeare quotation with a word blanked out.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet's line to Ophelia: wise men know well enough what horned freaks women make of them, meaning cuckolds.
explanation.definitionFit: Hideous or unnatural creatures, here the horned beasts a cuckold was said to become.

clue.text: Even a mule, with a little science, can develop it

definitions.text: Even a mule, with a little science, can develop it

indicators.note: the abbreviation is taken in among the animal's letters, so it goes along with the mule

parts.note: sc is a short form, a small piece, of the word science

explanation.surface: Even a stubborn beast of burden can build strength if trained scientifically.
explanation.definitionFit: Bodily strength and brawn, which a mule has and which training builds up.

clue.text: The morrow of a blue moon, perhaps

definitions.text: The morrow of a blue moon, perhaps

parts.words: The morrow of a blue moon, perhaps
parts.note: as Monday follows Sunday, the day after a once-in-a-blue-moon event is an indefinite future one

explanation.surface: Asks what follows a very rare occurrence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue moon' plays on the phrase 'once in a blue moon'; its morrow is some vague future time, formed like a weekday name.
explanation.definitionFit: At an unspecified future time, the vague 'one of these days' answer.

clue.text: Hungarian patriot

parts.note: Lajos ... led Hungary's 1848 revolution against Austrian rule

explanation.surface: A plain request for a famous Magyar nationalist.
explanation.definitionFit: Lajos, the 1848 revolutionary leader and regent-president of Hungary, celebrated as its national hero.

clue.text: As we go for a very little change on Lake Ontario

indicators.note: only one letter is swapped, the smallest change possible to the phrase

explanation.surface: A traveller noting small changes on a journey round the Great Lakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For a very little change' swaps just one letter: the first A of AS WE GO becomes O.
explanation.definitionFit: A port city in New York State on the southern shore of the lake.

clue.text: Material wreck

definitions.meaning: a coarse linen or cotton fabric used for towels and curtains

explanation.definitionFit: Both a coarse plain-weave fabric and a smash-up or collision.

clue.text: French husband surrounded by chores'

indicators.note: the French word sits with the chores wrapped all round it

parts.note: chores are tasks, jobs to be done
mari is French for husband

explanation.surface: A Frenchman buried under a pile of household jobs.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue as printed has no definition word; the trailing apostrophe suggests something was lost. The wordplay alone builds the answer: MARI inside TASKS.
explanation.definitionFit: No definition survives in the print; the answer is the plural of a feathery-leaved shrub of coasts and deserts.

clue.text: "O, will you cat no grapes my fox ?" (All's Well)

definitions.text: "O, will you cat no grapes my fox ?" (All's Well)

parts.words: "O, will you cat no grapes my fox ?" (All's Well)
parts.note: Lafeu teases the King in All's Well That Ends Well: will you eat no grapes, my kingly fox, the word missing before fox

explanation.surface: A Shakespeare line about a fox refusing grapes, with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed 'cat' is 'eat'; the gap before 'fox' takes the adjective Lafeu uses to the King, since sour grapes are the fox's fable.
explanation.definitionFit: Kingly, fitting a monarch, as the addressed fox here is the King himself.

clue.text: Naaman was before seven immersions

parts.note: in 2 Kings, the Syrian captain Naaman was cured of his skin disease by dipping seven times in the Jordan

explanation.surface: A Bible story told as a riddle about what Naaman used to be.
explanation.walkthrough: Elisha told Naaman to wash seven times in the Jordan; before that he suffered from the disease of the skin.
explanation.definitionFit: One suffering from the skin disease that afflicted Naaman until healed in the river.

clue.text: Nothing doing for soldiers in India? Just the converse

definitions.text: Nothing doing for soldiers in India? Just the converse

parts.words: Nothing doing for soldiers in India? Just the converse
parts.note: the city was a major military cantonment of the Raj, a busy station with plenty for troops to do

explanation.surface: Asks whether soldiers posted to India had nothing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: The city near Bombay was a large army station of British India, busy rather than idle; the old spelling is used.
explanation.definitionFit: The old spelling of Pune, the Indian city that was a big Raj army cantonment.

clue.text: Not one of the R.A.F. Boffins

definitions.text: Not one of the R.A.F. Boffins

parts.words: Not one of the R.A.F. Boffins
parts.note: boffins were the clever back-room experts, so the opposite is a simpleton, also the name of a tropical seabird

explanation.surface: Someone who failed to make the Air Force's team of scientific experts.
explanation.walkthrough: Boffins were wartime RAF slang for brainy experts; the answer is a fool, and punningly a bird, fitting an air force.
explanation.definitionFit: A simpleton or fool, and also a tern of tropical seas, thought stupidly tame.

clue.text: Stolen ice (anag.)

indicators.note: the bracketed abbreviation for anagram tells the solver to rearrange the two words before it

explanation.surface: Hints at a theft from the cold store.
explanation.walkthrough: A bare '(anag.)' clue in 1940s Times style: no definition is given, just the letters of STOLEN ICE to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: There is no separate definition; the letters make the word for polls in which voters choose representatives.

clue.text: That touch of jaundice that makes for cowardice

definitions.text: That touch of jaundice that makes for cowardice

parts.words: That touch of jaundice that makes for cowardice
parts.note: jaundice turns the skin a pale gold colour, and a cowardly person is said to have a band of that colour down the back

explanation.surface: A medical-sounding claim that a liver ailment causes timidity.
explanation.walkthrough: Jaundice colours the skin; the idiom for a cowardly trait uses the same colour as a stripe.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for a cowardly streak in someone's character.
